perturbation-parameter.idea: A weak change can be estimated from a problem we already know how to solve.
perturbation-parameter.explanation: Start with two energy levels. Their gap is the difference between their energies. A new interaction can link the levels. Compare the strength of that link with the gap. When the link is much smaller, a first estimate based on the old levels can work well.

example.title: A weak two-level coupling
steps: The gap is 4 eV and the coupling is 0.20 eV, so their ratio is 0.05.
The lower shift is approximately −0.20²/4 = −0.0100 eV; the exact model gives about −0.009975 eV.

perturbation-parameter.equation: smallness ratio = coupling size / energy gap

terms.definition: A change added to a reference model.
One amount divided by another. Three red counters for every two blue gives a red-to-blue ratio of 3/2.

first-energy-shift.idea: We can estimate how far a small change moves an energy level before solving the whole problem again.
first-energy-shift.explanation: Keep the old state for a first calculation. Use it to find the average extra energy from the change. This shortcut applies to a level clearly separated from the others. Doubling a weak change doubles this first estimate.

example.title: A small diagonal change
steps: The first coefficient is 0.6 eV and the change parameter is 0.10.
The first shift is 0.060 eV, taking the reference energy 1 eV to 1.060 eV.

first-energy-shift.equation: first energy shift = change strength × original-state average of the added energy

first-state-shift.idea: A weak link between two energy states can give each a little of the other state’s wave pattern.
first-state-shift.explanation: Divide the strength of the link by the difference between the old energies. This estimates the amount mixed into the original wave. Its sign tells how the patterns combine. To get a chance, square its size.

example.title: A small admixture
steps: A 0.20 eV coupling links a zero-energy state to one at 5 eV.
The approximate state is |0⟩ − 0.04|1⟩. The small component’s weight is about 0.0016 before normalization.

first-state-shift.equation: mixing amplitude ≈ coupling / signed energy gap

terms.definition: The two normalized reference energy states.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.

second-energy-shift.idea: A nearby level can change the energy of a state even when the simplest estimate misses the change.
second-energy-shift.explanation: The link between states enters this next correction twice, so doubling a weak link makes the correction four times as large. Divide the squared link by the signed energy difference. For the lowest level, all the other levels lie above it, and these corrections push its energy down.

example.title: Two higher-state contributions
steps: Couplings 0.6 eV and 0.8i eV connect the ground state to levels 3 and 8 eV above it.
The coefficient is −0.6²/3 − 0.8²/8 = −0.20 eV. At λ = 0.25, the contribution is −0.0125 eV.

second-energy-shift.equation: second contribution = λ² Σ coupling size² / signed gap

terms.definition: The dimensionless strength parameter.
Add the contributions from the other reference states.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.
A state with the lowest allowed energy.

perturbation-normalization.idea: Normalizing an approximation does not supply its missing physics.
perturbation-normalization.explanation: Divide the chosen approximate vector by its length so its probabilities add to one. This corrects its size, but cannot recover other state components that the approximation left out.

example.title: Normalizing a two-part guess
steps: Use |0⟩ − 0.06|1⟩. Its squared norm is 1.0036.
Divide by √1.0036. The second-state probability becomes 0.0036/1.0036, about 0.003587.

perturbation-normalization.equation: normalized vector = trial vector / its length

terms.definition: The two orthogonal normalized reference states.
A list of components that can be added and scaled together. A familiar example is a displacement arrow with length and direction.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.
A result close enough to use when the stated conditions hold. For example, treating a nearly flat road as level can simplify a short-trip calculation.

perturbation-error-check.idea: Compare an approximation with a solvable case to measure its error.
perturbation-error-check.explanation: State what your error is measured against. A relative error divides by a chosen reference value, so it is undefined when that reference is zero even if absolute error is zero.

example.title: Checking a second-order shift
steps: For gap 2 eV and coupling 0.20 eV, the estimate is −0.020000 eV; the exact shift is about −0.019804 eV.
The absolute difference is about 0.000196 eV, roughly 0.99% of the exact shift’s size.

terms.definition: A result close enough to use when the stated conditions hold. For example, treating a nearly flat road as level can simplify a short-trip calculation.

project-perturbation.idea: When two states start at exactly the same energy, calculate their response to a change together.
project-perturbation.explanation: The usual shortcut divides by the difference between the two energies. Here that difference is zero. Instead, write down how the new interaction connects the tied states. Find the combinations that have definite energies after the change.

example.title: Splitting a tied pair
steps: Two states both start at 2 eV. Their restricted perturbation has coefficients +0.5 and −0.5 eV.
At strength 0.10, the first-order energies become 2.05 and 1.95 eV.

project-perturbation.equation: new energy ≈ shared energy + change strength × block eigenvalue

terms.definition: The energy matrix restricted to the tied states.
The multiplier for a state whose shape the matrix preserves.

diagonalize-degenerate-block.idea: When two waves combine, their timing matters as much as their sizes.
diagonalize-degenerate-block.explanation: Suppose two states have the same energy until a new interaction links them. Its entries can include i, the number whose square is −1. That part records how the waves line up. Replacing it with its size discards information and can predict the wrong combination of states.

example.title: A complex two-state block
steps: Use [[1,2i],[−2i,1]] meV. The vector (i,1)/√2 has eigenvalue 3 meV.
For shared energy 10 meV and strength 0.20, this branch shifts to 10.6 meV.

terms.definition: The shared reference energy.
An eigenvalue of the full complex perturbation block.
Change strength.
One thousandth of an electronvolt.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.
A list of components that can be added and scaled together. A familiar example is a displacement arrow with length and direction.
The number that a matrix or other linear rule multiplies a matching eigenvector by.

near-degenerate-block.idea: Two levels with almost the same energy can mix strongly even when their link is small.
near-degenerate-block.explanation: Compare the link with the gap, the difference between their energies. If they are similar in size, calculate both levels together. Check any levels you left out before trusting the result.

example.title: A close pair
steps: The average energy is 5 eV, the bare splitting 0.20 eV and coupling 0.15 eV.
The block energies are 5 ± √(0.10² + 0.15²), about 4.81972 and 5.18028 eV.

terms.definition: Average reference energy.
Uncoupled splitting.
Coupling energy.
The two energies after solving the coupled pair.

symmetry-and-splitting.idea: Two waves can keep their separate shapes while their energies shift by different amounts.
symmetry-and-splitting.explanation: Flip the position coordinate, like reflecting a drawing in a mirror. An even wave keeps the same value and an odd wave changes sign. A change that stays the same under this reflection cannot mix the two shapes. It can still move their energy levels apart.

example.title: No mixing, but a split
steps: An even perturbation gives coefficients 0.2 and −0.1 eV to a tied even/odd pair.
At strength 0.50, their shifts are +0.10 and −0.05 eV, separating them by 0.15 eV.

symmetry-and-splitting.equation: separation = difference between the two energy shifts

terms.definition: Unchanged or sign-reversed when reflected.

variational-bound.idea: An allowed trial state gives an energy at least as high as the ground energy.
variational-bound.explanation: Its energy average combines possible energies with nonnegative weights. None lies below the lowest, so the average cannot either; the trial must satisfy the model’s boundaries and have finite energy.

example.title: A trial energy average
steps: Energy-basis weights 0.50,0.25,0.25 multiply energies 1,3,7 eV.
The average is 3 eV. This gives an upper bound on the ground energy, not proof that it equals 3 eV.

terms.definition: An allowed candidate chosen to estimate the true state.

gaussian-trial-energy.idea: A wave squeezed into a narrow space pays one energy cost. A broad wave can pay another.
gaussian-trial-energy.explanation: Try a bell-shaped wave in a trap whose potential energy rises steeply away from the centre. A narrow wave has a larger spread of momentum and more kinetic energy. A broad wave reaches the costly outer parts of the trap. Add both energies to compare widths.

example.title: A Gaussian with scaled width one
steps: At width ratio β = 1, the kinetic contribution is 0.25E_s and potential contribution 0.75E_s.
If E_s = 0.20 eV, the total trial energy is 0.20 eV.

terms.definition: Gaussian width divided by the fixed trap length scale.
The fixed energy scale of this quartic-trap model.
The average energy of the chosen trial state.
A potential energy growing as position to the fourth power.
Energy associated with an arrangement, such as the height of a weight above the floor.
Energy an object has because it is moving.
One amount divided by another. Three red counters for every two blue gives a red-to-blue ratio of 3/2.

minimize-trial-width.idea: Find the best width within the trial family without calling it exact.
minimize-trial-width.explanation: Vary the width while keeping the trap fixed. The minimum is the best energy bound this family supplies; another allowed shape may still improve it.

example.title: Optimizing the quartic-trap Gaussian
steps: The best width ratio is 6^(−1/6), about 0.74184.
The trial energy is about 0.68142E_s, or 0.13628 eV when E_s = 0.20 eV.

terms.definition: The fixed energy scale of this quartic-trap model.
One amount divided by another. Three red counters for every two blue gives a red-to-blue ratio of 3/2.

ritz-subspace.idea: More allowed trial shapes can improve an energy bound.
ritz-subspace.explanation: Combine the allowed shapes and minimize their average energy. If every old choice remains available, the new minimum cannot rise: the previous best is still an option. The result remains a bound, not a claim of an exact energy.

example.title: Mixing two trial shapes
steps: Two orthonormal shapes give energy matrix [[2,−0.3],[−0.3,5]] eV.
Its lowest eigenvalue is about 1.97029 eV, improving the first shape’s 2 eV bound.

terms.definition: Normalized and having zero overlap with each other.
The multiplier for a state whose shape the energy matrix preserves.
A grid of numbers. In these calculations it can act as a rule that turns one list of numbers into another.

orthogonal-excited-trial.idea: To estimate an excited level, first rule out all the lower levels.
orthogonal-excited-trial.explanation: An excited level has energy above the lowest level. A trial wave can contain a mixture of levels. Any lower level in the mix can pull its average down. Require zero overlap with every lower exact state before using the average as an upper limit for the level you want.

example.title: Bounding the first excited energy
steps: Exact energies are 0,2,6 eV. Choose weights 0.75 and 0.25 only on the last two.
The average is 3 eV, a valid upper bound on the first excited energy because no ground component remains.

orthogonal-excited-trial.equation: trial energy ≥ target energy when all lower-state overlaps are zero

terms.definition: One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.

wkb-local-wave-number.idea: A wave moving through a gently changing region can have a different wavelength at each place.
wkb-local-wave-number.explanation: Wavelength is the distance spanned by one cycle. The WKB method breaks the path into small pieces and counts how far the cycle advances in each. This works when the wavelength changes little over one cycle and the particle stays away from a turning point.

example.title: One point in an allowed region
steps: The local kinetic energy is 0.40 eV. With the chosen mass and length scales, its wave number is 1 per nanometre.
The local wavelength is 2π/k, about 6.283 nm. The potential must still change slowly for WKB to apply.

terms.definition: Local phase change per unit distance.
An approximation for waves in slowly varying regions.
The distance along a wave from one point to the matching point in the next cycle, such as crest to crest.
Energy an object has because it is moving.

wkb-slow-variation.idea: A wave shortcut works best when its spacing barely changes over one cycle.
wkb-slow-variation.explanation: Wave number measures how quickly a wave passes through a cycle as you move along it. The WKB method treats each short piece like a wave with nearly fixed wave number. Near a turning point the wave number approaches zero, and this test can fail.

example.title: Near the turn in a linear potential
steps: For this model, the turning point is at scaled position 4. At position 3.9, the check is 1/[2(4 − 3.9)^(3/2)].
That is about 15.81, far from small. Ordinary WKB should not be trusted there.

terms.definition: Local wave number.
Its change per unit distance.
Position divided by the model’s length scale.
One amount divided by another. Three red counters for every two blue gives a red-to-blue ratio of 3/2.

wkb-amplitude-current.idea: A slower wave needs more probability packed into each metre to carry the same flow.
wkb-amplitude-current.explanation: Think of cars moving through a gate. If they slow down, they must be closer together for just as many to pass each minute. In one traveling wave the same arithmetic connects speed, probability density and flow. This WKB shortcut breaks down at the point where classical motion would turn around.

example.title: Keeping one branch’s flow fixed
steps: Momentum falls from 4p_ref to p_ref. Initial density is 0.10 per nanometre.
Density rises fourfold to 0.40 per nanometre, leaving momentum times density unchanged.

terms.definition: A positive reference momentum.

wkb-forbidden-action.idea: Inside a barrier, a decaying wave can become very small without becoming zero.
wkb-forbidden-action.explanation: The decay builds up across the distance traveled through the barrier. This tells us how amplitude changes inside; finding transmission through the whole barrier also requires matching the waves at its edges.

example.title: One nanometre inside a barrier
steps: The amplitude shrinks by a factor e^(−2) across 1 nm, about 0.135.
The probability density shrinks by its square, e^(−4), about 0.0183.

terms.definition: The wave quantity whose squared size gives probability density.
The number about 2.718 used for exponential change.
Chance per small interval or region. Add the density over a region to find the chance of detecting the particle there.

simple-turning-point.idea: A wave needs special care near the place where a classical particle would turn back.
simple-turning-point.explanation: At this turning point the potential energy reaches the particle’s total energy. A shortcut for slowly changing waves gives an unreasonable size near that point. For a smooth crossing with a nonzero slope, a shape called an Airy function joins the waves on the two sides while staying finite.

example.title: Measuring distance from the turn
steps: For this model, the turning-point length scale is 2 nm.
A point 8 nm to the right has scaled distance 8/2 = 4. This labels its position; it does not by itself prove an approximation accurate.

simple-turning-point.equation: scaled distance = distance from turning point / local length scale

terms.definition: A wave shape that solves the equation near a smooth, sloping turning point.
Energy associated with an arrangement, such as the height of a weight above the floor.
How much a graph rises or falls for each step to the right.
A result close enough to use when the stated conditions hold. For example, treating a nearly flat road as level can simplify a short-trip calculation.

wkb-two-turning-quantization.idea: A wave trapped between two smooth turning points fits only at certain energies.
wkb-two-turning-quantization.explanation: A turning point is where the total energy meets the potential energy. Inside, the wave repeats. Outside, it fades. The smooth turn at each end changes the timing of its cycles. Counting these shifts explains the half-step in the WKB energy rule.

example.title: A harmonic trap level
steps: The energy spacing is 0.080 eV. Choose level number n = 2.
Its energy is (2 + ½) × 0.080 = 0.200 eV. WKB gives the exact energies for this special harmonic trap.

terms.definition: The level number, starting at zero.
A wave approximation used away from turning points and joined to suitable local solutions.

wkb-tunnelling-validity.idea: A particle has a small chance of passing through some barriers even when its energy is below the barrier top.
wkb-tunnelling-validity.explanation: The wave fades as it extends across a barrier. The WKB estimate adds up this fading over many small pieces to predict how much gets through. It works best when the wave fades strongly and the two turning points are well separated.

example.title: A smooth parabolic barrier
steps: The barrier calculation gives a decay measure S/ℏ = 1.5π, about 4.712.
The leading transmission is e^(−3π), about 0.0000807, or 0.00807%. This leaves out finer corrections.

terms.definition: The total dimensionless decay measure through the barrier.
e raised to x, with e about 2.718.

relativistic-kinetic-expansion.idea: At low momentum, relativity slightly lowers the usual kinetic-energy estimate.
relativistic-kinetic-expansion.explanation: The familiar momentum-squared rule is the first part of an expansion. Its next correction is negative; this shortened formula is useful only when momentum is much smaller than mass times light speed.

example.title: Momentum equal to 0.2mc
steps: The usual energy is 0.0200mc² and the first correction is −0.0002mc².
Their sum is 0.0198mc², close to the exact 0.0198039mc².

terms.definition: Kinetic energy.
Momentum size.
Rest mass.
Light speed.

coulomb-moment-bridge.idea: To find an average distance from the nucleus, count the space around it in thin shells.
coulomb-moment-bridge.explanation: A shell twice as far from the centre has four times as much area. For equally thin shells, that means four times as much space. Along with the squared size of the radial wave, count this radius-squared factor to find each shell’s share.

example.title: An inverse-cube average for a 2p state
steps: Using the supplied 2p radial wave gives an average of 1/r³ equal to 1/(24a³).
The same calculation cannot be copied to an s state: its inverse-cube average diverges at the center.

terms.definition: Distance from the center.
Radial amplitude when the angular part is normalized.
A very small shell thickness.
The Coulomb model’s length scale.

atomic-spin-orbit.idea: An electron’s built-in spin and its motion around the nucleus can shift its energy together.
atomic-spin-orbit.explanation: Spin is a quantum property measured along an axis. The electron wave around a nucleus also carries angular momentum. How the two combine helps set the energy shift. This formula assumes nonzero orbital angular momentum. A state with zero orbital angular momentum needs separate treatment.

example.title: The 2p, j = 3/2 level
steps: For this level, the model gives a shift K₀/96.
With K₀ = 1.45 meV, the shift is about +0.01510 meV.

atomic-spin-orbit.equation: energy shift = K₀/96 for this 2p branch

terms.definition: The model’s fixed energy scale.
The total angular-momentum label.
One thousandth of an electronvolt.
An intrinsic quantum form of angular momentum.

contact-darwin-shift.idea: One small correction to an atom’s energy depends on the electron wave right at the nucleus.
contact-darwin-shift.explanation: In this calculation the nucleus is treated as a point. A mathematical tool called a delta function selects the probability density exactly there when we add over space. Density is chance per small volume. It can have a value at the centre even though a single point occupies zero volume.

example.title: The 1s contact correction
steps: For the supplied 1s wave, the model gives a correction K₀/2.
At K₀ = 1.45 meV, the shift is +0.725 meV. This is one contribution to the energy.

terms.definition: The fixed energy scale in this Coulomb model.
A mathematical rule that picks out a value at a point inside an integral.
One thousandth of an electronvolt.
Chance per small interval or region. Add the density over a region to find the chance of detecting the particle there.

hydrogen-fine-structure.idea: Some hydrogen energy levels split into closely spaced levels when we include small effects.
hydrogen-fine-structure.explanation: One change refines the energy of motion. Another links an electron’s spin to its motion around the nucleus. A third depends on its wave at the nucleus. Add the changes for the same state. Some energies still match in this model, which holds the nucleus fixed.

example.title: Adding the 2s corrections
steps: The kinetic correction is −13K₀/128 and the contact correction is +K₀/16; the spin–orbit term is zero.
The sum is −5K₀/128. For K₀ = 1.45 meV, it is about −0.05664 meV.

terms.definition: The model’s fixed energy scale.
One thousandth of an electronvolt.
An additional small atomic energy shift beyond this model.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.

weak-zeeman.idea: A weak magnetic field can split energy readings that matched without the field.
weak-zeeman.explanation: An electron has its own spin, and its wave can also carry angular momentum around the nucleus. In this lesson the link between the two is stronger than the magnetic change. Treat them as one combined quantity, then find its component along the field.

example.title: One 2p magnetic level
steps: For j = 3/2 and component label m_j = 3/2, the response factor is 4/3.
At 0.01 T, the shift is 2μ_BB, about +1.1576 × 10⁻⁶ eV. This is small compared with the stated spin–orbit gap.

weak-zeeman.equation: energy shift = μ_B B g_j m_j

terms.definition: The positive Bohr magneton, a magnetic energy-per-field scale.
Magnetic-field strength.
The level’s magnetic response factor.
The numbered total-angular-momentum component along the field.
Total angular-momentum label.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.
A field that can turn a compass and push sideways on a moving electric charge.

strong-zeeman.idea: A stronger magnetic field can make two separate spin and orbital labels more useful than a single combined label.
strong-zeeman.explanation: A field changes the energies associated with the electron’s spin and its motion around the nucleus. If this energy change is much larger than the link between spin and motion, count their along-field contributions separately. The model still has an upper limit on the field it can describe.

example.title: Cancellation of the leading magnetic shift
steps: At 20 T, choose orbital component m_l = 1 and spin component m_s = −½.
The factor m_l + 2m_s equals zero, so the leading magnetic shift vanishes. Smaller corrections may remain.

terms.definition: The positive Bohr magneton.
Magnetic-field strength.
The numbered orbital and spin components along the field.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.
A field that can turn a compass and push sideways on a moving electric charge.

zeeman-crossover.idea: When two effects are close in strength, dropping either can predict the wrong atomic energies.
zeeman-crossover.explanation: One effect links electron spin to its motion around the nucleus. The other comes from an applied magnetic field. Put the possible states and the links between them into one small table of numbers. Solving that table keeps both effects.

example.title: A two-state crossover model
steps: The model matrix is [[3,√2],[√2,−1]] in microelectronvolts.
Its energies are 1 ± √6, about 3.449 and −1.449 microelectronvolts. Their sum, 2, matches the matrix’s diagonal sum.

terms.definition: The higher and lower energies of this two-state model.
One millionth of an electronvolt.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.
A grid of numbers. In these calculations it can act as a rule that turns one list of numbers into another.

quadratic-stark-parity.idea: Doubling a weak electric field can make a level’s energy shift about four times as much.
quadratic-stark-parity.explanation: For this symmetric state, opposite sides balance, so the change directly proportional to the field is zero. The field can still mix in a state with a different reflection pattern. The next change depends on the field strength squared.

example.title: Mixing with one higher state
steps: A higher state lies 4 meV above the lower state, and the field coupling is 0.2 meV.
The lower shift is approximately −0.2²/4 = −0.010 meV. This two-state estimate is not the full hydrogen response.

quadratic-stark-parity.equation: lower energy shift ≈ −coupling² / positive energy gap

terms.definition: One thousandth of an electronvolt.
Proportional to the square of the small field strength.
A rule for the force per unit positive charge at a place. Its direction is the way a small positive test charge would be pushed.

linear-stark-subspace.idea: An electric field can split two tied energy levels as soon as the field is turned on.
linear-stark-subspace.explanation: The two states start at the same energy but have different wave patterns under reflection. The field can mix them into two new combinations. Solve for the two together. A shortcut that divides by their starting energy gap would divide by zero.

example.title: An ideal hydrogen n = 2 pair
steps: For the chosen field, the 2s–2p coupling has size 0.012 meV.
The new combinations shift by +0.012 and −0.012 meV, leaving a gap of 0.024 meV. Finer atomic effects are omitted here.

linear-stark-subspace.equation: splitting of this tied pair = 2 × coupling size

terms.definition: One thousandth of an electronvolt.
Hydrogen’s main energy-level number.
A rule for the force per unit positive charge at a place. Its direction is the way a small positive test charge would be pushed.

minimal-coupling.idea: In a magnetic field, two different quantities can carry the name momentum.
minimal-coupling.explanation: One, called canonical momentum, comes from how the wave changes with position. The other, called kinetic momentum, is linked to actual motion. To find it, subtract the charge times a field-related quantity called the vector potential from the canonical momentum.

example.title: A constant vector potential
steps: The canonical momentum is 4p₀ and charge times vector potential is p₀.
The kinetic momentum is 4p₀ − p₀ = 3p₀.

terms.definition: Canonical momentum.
Particle charge.
Magnetic vector potential, part of the mathematical description of the field.
A positive reference momentum.
A list of components that can be added and scaled together. A familiar example is a displacement arrow with length and direction.
A field that can turn a compass and push sideways on a moving electric charge.

gauge-state-phase.idea: Different sets of numbers can describe the same electric and magnetic fields.
gauge-state-phase.explanation: One choice of these numbers is called a gauge. If you change the choice, adjust the phase of the wave too. Phase tells how wave parts line up. Use both changes together, and quantities you can measure, such as momentum related to motion, still agree.

example.title: The same motion in two descriptions
steps: Initially, canonical momentum is 4p₀ and charge times vector potential is p₀.
After the matching change they are 6p₀ and 3p₀. Both give kinetic momentum 3p₀.

terms.definition: A positive reference momentum.
A coordinated change of potentials and wave phase that preserves physical predictions.
A list of components that can be added and scaled together. A familiar example is a displacement arrow with length and direction.
A field that can turn a compass and push sideways on a moving electric charge.

flux-loop-phase.idea: A magnetic field enclosed by two paths can shift where their waves reinforce or cancel.
flux-loop-phase.explanation: Imagine two possible routes around a region containing magnetic field. Magnetic flux measures the field passing through the enclosed surface. It can change which part of one wave cycle meets which part of the other. Recombining the routes can then change the detector’s chance of a hit.

example.title: A quarter flux unit
steps: For an electron and flux h/(4e), the signed phase difference is −π/2.
For equal path amplitudes and no other phase difference, the chosen output probability is (1 + cos(−π/2))/2 = ½.

terms.definition: The phase difference between the two paths.
Planck’s constant.
The positive size of the electron’s charge.
Having a stable relative phase so amplitudes can interfere.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
A field that can turn a compass and push sideways on a moving electric charge.

landau-oscillator-map.idea: A charged particle moving in a plane can have evenly spaced energies in a uniform magnetic field.
landau-oscillator-map.explanation: Here we leave out spin. The equation for motion across the magnetic field has the same form as one for a quantum spring. Its levels make equal energy steps. Different labels can place the wave in different parts of the plane while keeping the same energy.

example.title: A 6 meV level spacing
steps: With spacing 6 meV, the lowest level has energy 3 meV.
The next levels are 9 and 15 meV. This model leaves out spin, edges and interactions.

terms.definition: The level number, starting at zero.
One thousandth of an electronvolt.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.
A field that can turn a compass and push sideways on a moving electric charge.

lessonCopy.example.steps.0: Choose a model whose spacing ℏωc=6 meV. The first three planar energies are 3,9 and 15 meV.
lessonCopy.check.prompt: With spacing 8 meV, what is the n=2 planar energy?
lessonCopy.practice.parts.2.label: n=3 energy with spacing 4 meV

instantaneous-eigenstates.idea: If your measuring directions turn while you measure, their turning must enter the calculation.
instantaneous-eigenstates.explanation: At each instant, the energy rule picks out wave patterns with definite energies. Those patterns can change as the rule changes. A wave described using these moving reference patterns can acquire new shares of each. Count both the changing references and the wave’s own change.

example.title: A rotating two-state basis
steps: The basis angle changes at 0.6 radians per second. The relevant overlap rate is half of that, 0.3 per second.
Starting in the upper reference state gives a lower-component amplitude rate of −0.3 per second at that instant. This is not a probability.

instantaneous-eigenstates.equation: overlap rate = basis-angle rate / 2 for this spin basis

terms.definition: Reference states used to describe another state.
The energy rule that controls quantum evolution.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

adiabatic-gap-criterion.idea: A state can follow a slowly changing energy level when other nearby levels stay far enough away.
adiabatic-gap-criterion.explanation: The energy gap is the difference between two possible energies. Compare how quickly the reference patterns change with how quickly this gap changes their relative timing. A small ratio supports following one level. Check it all along the path because the smallest gap may come later.

example.title: A slowly rotating spin model
steps: The basis rotates at 0.4 radians per second and the gap frequency is 20 radians per second.
The check gives 0.4/(2 × 20) = 0.01. This supports slow following locally, without proving it for the whole experiment.

adiabatic-gap-criterion.equation: local check = rotation rate / (2 × gap frequency)

terms.definition: The energy difference divided by ℏ.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
Staying close to the corresponding changing energy state.
For a repeating signal, the number of cycles per second. Five cycles each second is 5 hertz.

dynamic-geometric-phase.idea: A quantum wave’s place in its cycle can change for two reasons during a slow journey.
dynamic-geometric-phase.explanation: Energy advances the cycle as time passes. A changing reference state can add a second shift that depends on the path taken. This is called geometric phase. Compare the end wave with the starting reference consistently when predicting a measurable difference.

example.title: One smooth segment
steps: The energy contribution is −1.5 radians and the geometric contribution is +0.3 radians.
Their sum is −1.2 radians in this chosen description. This segment is not a closed-loop claim.

dynamic-geometric-phase.equation: total phase in this description = dynamical phase + geometric contribution

terms.definition: The angle that controls how complex amplitudes add.

adiabatic-spin-check.idea: How often would a spin fail to follow a slowly turning magnetic field?
adiabatic-spin-check.explanation: Start with the spin in one of the two states selected by the field. At the end, measure along the new field direction. Getting the other energy state counts as failure to follow. The exact chance in this small model checks the shortcut that assumes perfect following.

example.title: Checking a rotating field
steps: The gap frequency is 4 radians per second and the field turns at 1 radian per second.
At time π/√17 seconds, the failure probability reaches 1/(4² + 1²) = 1/17, about 5.88%.

adiabatic-spin-check.equation: maximum failure probability = rotation rate² / (gap frequency² + rotation rate²)

terms.definition: Energy separation divided by ℏ.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.
For a repeating signal, the number of cycles per second. Five cycles each second is 5 hertz.

berry-spin-loop.idea: Returning a magnetic field to its original direction can leave a change in a wave’s timing.
berry-spin-loop.explanation: Trace the field direction as a point moving on a sphere of radius one. Here the spin stays in its positive state while the point makes a slow loop. The geometric phase is minus half the loop’s signed area. Compare this wave with a reference wave to detect the change.

example.title: A cone with a 60° opening angle
steps: The direction loop encloses solid angle π.
The positive eigenstate gains geometric phase −π/2, or −90°. The sign belongs to the specified loop direction.

terms.definition: Area on a sphere of radius one, measured in steradians.
The state with positive energy for the stated two-state Hamiltonian.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.
A state that gives one definite result for the chosen ideal measurement.

born-oppenheimer-factor.idea: Electrons in a molecule often adjust much faster than its nuclei move.
born-oppenheimer-factor.explanation: A nucleus is a heavy centre of an atom. For each arrangement of nuclei, first hold them still and calculate an electron energy. Follow how this energy changes from place to place to estimate the nuclear motion. If two electron energies get close, the one-state shortcut can fail.

example.title: Building one point on a molecular energy surface
steps: At one nuclear position, electronic energy is −4 eV and nuclear repulsion is +1.5 eV.
The leading potential for nuclear motion is −2.5 eV there. Other positions must be calculated to learn the surface’s shape.

born-oppenheimer-factor.equation: nuclear potential ≈ electronic energy + nuclear repulsion

terms.definition: The potential energy assigned to each nuclear arrangement.

nuclear-effective-surface.idea: The atoms of a molecule can vibrate like weights connected by a spring.
nuclear-effective-surface.explanation: Near a stable arrangement, moving the nuclei a little raises the energy. A steeper, more curved energy bowl makes a stronger restoring force. That stiffness and the masses set the vibration rate for small movements. Pulling the molecule apart goes beyond the spring model.

example.title: A small vibration near the minimum
steps: With mass 2 × 10⁻²⁶ kg and curvature 8 N/m, the angular frequency is 2 × 10¹³ per second.
The quantum spacing is about 0.01316 eV. The lowest level lies half that spacing above the minimum.

terms.definition: How sharply the potential energy bends upward near its minimum.
How quickly a cycle advances, measured in radians per second. One whole turn is 2π radians.

nonadiabatic-boundaries.idea: Moving a molecule’s nuclei can change which energy an electron will have when measured.
nonadiabatic-boundaries.explanation: The nuclei are the heavy centres of the atoms. As they move, the electron wave patterns can change and mix. The energy gap is the difference between two possible electron energies. Compare the strength of the mixing with that gap. When the gap is small, following just one pattern can give a poor prediction.

example.title: A local electronic mixing check
steps: For the given nuclear speed and changing electronic state, the coupling scale is 2.63285 × 10⁻⁵ eV.
Divide by the 0.02 eV gap to get about 0.001316. This is a small local warning ratio, not a complete error bound.

nonadiabatic-boundaries.equation: local mixing check = motion-induced coupling energy / electronic energy gap

terms.definition: Electronic energy viewed as a function of nuclear position.
One amount divided by another. Three red counters for every two blue gives a red-to-blue ratio of 3/2.

interaction-picture.idea: A calculation can be easier if you first take out a change you already know how to predict.
interaction-picture.explanation: For example, a wave may already change its timing even before a new interaction starts. The interaction picture builds that known motion into the reference used for the calculation. Adjust both the state and the measurement rule to keep the same predictions.

example.title: A changing off-diagonal coupling
steps: A constant reference gap gives frequency 2 radians per second. At time π/4 seconds, the interaction-picture coupling picks up phase i.
One off-diagonal entry is ig and the reverse is −ig, keeping the energy matrix Hermitian.

terms.definition: The real coupling energy in this example.
Reference energy-gap frequency.
Time.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.
Equal to the complex-conjugate transpose, as required for this energy matrix.
A complex phase factor with angle ωt.
A grid of numbers. In these calculations it can act as a rule that turns one list of numbers into another.
For a repeating signal, the number of cycles per second. Five cycles each second is 5 hertz.

first-transition-amplitude.idea: A brief, weak interaction can give a quantum system a small chance to change states.
first-transition-amplitude.explanation: Each moment adds a little wave contribution with its own timing. Add these contributions first, and then square the size to get a chance. The first estimate leaves out repeated jumps between states, so use it while leaving the starting state is still unlikely.

example.title: A short equal-energy coupling
steps: The coupling divided by ℏ is 0.04 per second and lasts 3 seconds.
The amplitude is −0.12i, so the transition probability is 0.12² = 0.0144, or 1.44%.

terms.definition: Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
The imaginary unit; multiplying by i changes phase, not size.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

finite-rectangular-pulse.idea: A pulse switched on for a short time can affect a wider range of energies than a long pulse.
finite-rectangular-pulse.explanation: A pulse is an interaction that lasts for a set time. Contributions from different moments can reinforce or cancel as their wave cycles advance. In the weak model here, a longer pulse makes the central response narrower in energy. The total chance of transfer must still be small.

example.title: A two-second pulse away from equal energies
steps: The coupling scale is 0.05 per second, the duration is 2 seconds and the gap frequency is π/2 radians per second.
The probability is 0.01 × (2/π)², about 0.00405, or 0.405%.

terms.definition: Transition probability.
Constant coupling energy.
Pulse duration.
Energy-gap frequency.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
sin(x)/x, defined as 1 at x = 0.
For a repeating signal, the number of cycles per second. Five cycles each second is 5 hertz.

harmonic-drive-terms.idea: A steadily repeating push can be described by two mathematical waves turning in opposite directions.
harmonic-drive-terms.explanation: Near resonance, the drive repeats close to the rate set by the energy difference. One wave then lines up for many cycles, while the other quickly changes its alignment. Add both before finding a probability unless their speeds and the pulse duration justify leaving the fast one out.

example.title: A particular resonant pulse
steps: The drive and gap frequencies are both 2 radians per second; the pulse lasts π seconds and g/ℏ = 0.02 per second.
The fast contribution cancels exactly for this duration. The remaining amplitude is −0.01πi, giving probability about 0.000987.

terms.definition: Transition probability.
Cosine-drive coupling energy.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
The imaginary unit.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
For a repeating signal, the number of cycles per second. Five cycles each second is 5 hertz.

dipole-selection-tests.idea: Symmetry can rule out some light-driven changes in an atom before you do the full calculation.
dipole-selection-tests.explanation: Compare the left and right sides of the wave overlap that couples the two states to light. If reflecting position reverses its sign, the two sides cancel when added. If they do not cancel by this test, other parts of the calculation still decide the chance.

example.title: Combining one radial and angular factor
steps: For the chosen z-directed transition, the radial factor is 0.30 nm and the angular factor is 1/√3.
Their product is about 0.1732 nm. This nonzero result includes both parts of the overlap.

dipole-selection-tests.equation: position overlap = radial factor × angular factor

terms.definition: The weighted comparison of the initial and final wave shapes.
Changing sign when position is reflected through the center.

weak-versus-rabi.idea: A weak-transition estimate fails once repeated transfers become important.
weak-versus-rabi.explanation: An exactly specified two-state coupling moves probability back and forth. The short-time estimate keeps only the beginning of that motion, so even weak coupling can outgrow the approximation if applied too long.

example.title: A small rotation angle
steps: For dimensionless angle a = 0.10, the weak estimate gives 0.0100.
The exact two-state result is sin²(0.10), about 0.0099667. Their difference is about 0.0000333.

terms.definition: Transition probability.
Coupling energy multiplied by time, then divided by ℏ.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
A result close enough to use when the stated conditions hold. For example, treating a nearly flat road as level can simplify a short-trip calculation.

density-of-final-states.idea: A density of states counts how many final states fit into an energy range.
density-of-final-states.explanation: In a large box, closely spaced levels can be averaged into a smooth count per energy. Multiply by a narrow energy width to estimate the count; a fractional average does not mean an individual state is a fraction.

example.title: A narrow energy window
steps: In the stated large-box model, the density is about 101.321 states per energy unit.
A width of 0.02 energy units contains an average of about 2.026 states in this smooth approximation.

density-of-final-states.equation: average number of states ≈ density per energy × energy width

terms.definition: Number of available states per small energy interval.
A result close enough to use when the stated conditions hold. For example, treating a nearly flat road as level can simplify a short-trip calculation.

long-time-pulse-window.idea: To estimate a steady rate, a pulse must last long enough to average over many suitable levels.
long-time-pulse-window.explanation: A very short pulse spreads its effect over a broad energy range. A very long one can pick out separate levels. Between those limits, the levels can act like a smooth group. The simple rate also assumes only a small chance of leaving the starting state.

example.title: Checking a one-second pulse
steps: The broad response time is 0.01 seconds, the level-resolution time is 100 seconds and the candidate rate is 0.02 per second.
A 1-second pulse sits between those times and transfers an estimated 0.02 probability. These checks support a possible rate window, not a precise error guarantee.

long-time-pulse-window.equation: short response time ≪ pulse duration ≪ level-resolution time

terms.definition: Much smaller than, by enough for the approximation being tested.

golden-rule-rate.idea: A quantum system can change state at a nearly steady rate when many final energies lie close together.
golden-rule-rate.explanation: Two things matter: how strongly the starting state links to each final state, and how many of those states fit in a small energy interval. More choices can raise the rate. This weak-link estimate works over a limited time and does not generally apply to just two isolated states.

example.title: A small continuum transition
steps: The supplied coupling and state density give a rate about 0.000152736 per picosecond.
Over 100 picoseconds, the estimated transfer probability is 0.01527, or 1.53%, provided the stated rate-window checks hold.

terms.definition: One trillionth of a second.
A smooth approximation to very closely spaced final states.

threshold-phase-space.idea: Sometimes an outcome becomes possible only after the energy passes a minimum.
threshold-phase-space.explanation: Think of the minimum as the threshold. In this model a free particle can move in three directions. Just above the threshold, the number of available states per energy grows like the square root of the extra energy. The rate follows this growth only if the link to those states changes little.

example.title: Raising the excess energy
steps: A model gives rate 0.03 per nanosecond at excess energy 0.04 eV.
At 0.09 eV, the rate grows by √(0.09/0.04) = 1.5, becoming 0.045 per nanosecond under the same coupling assumption.

threshold-phase-space.equation: rate ratio = √(new excess energy / old excess energy)

terms.definition: Energy above the minimum needed to open this final channel.
A square root answers “which number times itself gives this value?” The √ sign picks the zero or positive answer. For example, √9 = 3.
Something you take as true for a calculation, such as assuming that a cart’s speed stays steady.

rate-and-survival-limits.idea: Immediately after a state is prepared, the chance of leaving it need not grow at a steady rate.
rate-and-survival-limits.explanation: Survival means finding the system still in its starting state. If its spread of possible energies is finite, the initial chance of leaving grows with time squared. Doubling a very short time makes this chance about four times as large.

example.title: A very short observation
steps: The energy spread divided by ℏ is 2 per second, and the time is 0.01 seconds.
The leading survival estimate is 1 − 2² × 0.01² = 0.9996. Only about 0.04% is lost at this order.

terms.definition: Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
Probability of finding the initial state again.

electric-dipole-regime.idea: Light can push on a small atom almost uniformly even though the field changes across a whole wavelength.
electric-dipole-regime.explanation: A wavelength is one cycle measured in space. If the atom occupies only a tiny part of that cycle, its parts experience nearly the same electric field at a given time. This dipole approximation simplifies the pattern in space. A long or strong exposure can still cause a large change.

example.title: A small system in visible light
steps: The system size is 0.20 nm and the wavelength is 600 nm.
The phase-change check is 2π × 0.20/600, about 0.00209. This supports treating the field as nearly uniform across the system.

electric-dipole-regime.equation: spatial phase-change check = 2π × system size / wavelength

terms.definition: An interaction model using charge times position and a nearly uniform electric field.
The distance along a wave from one point to the matching point in the next cycle, such as crest to crest.

spontaneous-emission-input.idea: A decay rate predicts the average number of photons emitted by a group of atoms.
spontaneous-emission-input.explanation: A photon is one packet of light. In this model, each atom that still has extra energy has the same chance per second of giving it up as light. The number of atoms left with extra energy shrinks by the same fraction over equal times. That rule describes the group average. It does not give an exact emission time for one atom.

example.title: Five hundred independent excitations
steps: The decay rate is 0.4 per nanosecond. After 5 nanoseconds, the surviving fraction is e^(−2), about 0.1353.
The expected surviving count is about 67.7, leaving about 432.3 emitted photons on average. Actual counts are whole numbers and can vary.

spontaneous-emission-input.equation: expected survivors = initial count × exp(−rate × time)

terms.definition: e raised to x, with e about 2.718.
One billionth of a second.
One packet of electromagnetic radiation. Visible light and radio waves can both be described in photons.

stimulated-balance-inversion.idea: If light drives two energy levels equally well in both directions, it cannot steadily keep most atoms in the upper one in this model.
stimulated-balance-inversion.explanation: Light can lift a low-energy atom or bring a high-energy atom down. As more atoms reach the upper level, more can come down. Equal numbers balance these two flows. Atoms that fall on their own shift the balance toward the lower level.

example.title: Balancing two-level flows
steps: The stimulated rate is 0.3 per nanosecond and the spontaneous rate is 0.2 per nanosecond.
The steady excited fraction is 0.3/(2 × 0.3 + 0.2) = 0.375, or 37.5%.

terms.definition: Equal stimulated upward and downward rates.
Spontaneous downward rate.
No longer changing under the model’s constant rates.

environment-dephasing.idea: The surroundings can blur a quantum interference pattern without changing how often its two basic outcomes occur.
environment-dephasing.explanation: Different parts of a wave can leave different traces in the surroundings. If we ignore those traces, the parts no longer combine as strongly in our predictions. The separate outcome chances can stay the same even while their interference fades.

example.title: A partial environmental record
steps: Start with equal system amplitudes. The stated interaction gives the local matrix [[0.5,0.25],[0.25,0.5]].
Both populations remain 0.5, but coherence falls from 0.5 to 0.25. This finite environment does not guarantee permanent or steadily increasing loss.

environment-dephasing.equation: local coherence after interaction = initial coherence × cos θ

terms.definition: Off-diagonal state entries that carry relative-phase information.
The environment’s conditional rotation angle; here π/3.
A state described by one normalized quantum vector.
Wave contributions can strengthen or cancel when they meet. Quantum amplitudes can do this, too.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
A grid of numbers. In these calculations it can act as a rule that turns one list of numbers into another.

kraus-channel-bridge.idea: A rule for changing one quantum system must still make sense when that system is paired with another.
kraus-channel-bridge.explanation: A quantum channel is a rule that changes the table of predicted measurement results. Kraus matrices list possible changes whose combined action keeps the total chance at one. This construction also works when the two partners have linked quantum states.

example.title: A random phase flip
steps: Apply no phase flip with chance 0.8 and a phase flip with chance 0.2 to an equal superposition.
The output is [[0.5,0.3],[0.3,0.5]]. Populations stay fixed while coherence is multiplied by 0.6.

terms.definition: The phase-flip probability, between zero and one.
Matrices whose summed actions represent the quantum channel.
State entries that carry relative-phase information.
One quantum state formed by combining reference states with amplitudes. The parts can strengthen or cancel in a measurement.

amplitude-damping-channel.idea: When a quantum system loses energy, it becomes more likely to be found in its lowest-energy state.
amplitude-damping-channel.explanation: The chance of finding the higher energy is its excited-state population. If the outcome of a decay is unobserved, include both possibilities: the system decayed or it did not. The ground-state chance grows, and the link between the two wave amplitudes weakens. Shrinking the excited part alone would leave out the decay outcome.

example.title: A 36% decay chance
steps: Start from an equal superposition with ground and excited populations 0.5 each. Use decay probability 0.36.
The ground population becomes 0.68 and the excited population 0.32; coherence becomes 0.40. The populations still sum to one.

amplitude-damping-channel.equation: excited population after decay = (1 − p) × initial excited population

terms.definition: Decay probability during the chosen interval.
An off-diagonal entry carrying relative-phase information.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

markovian-decay-example.idea: Losing energy and losing the timing between wave parts are two different changes.
markovian-decay-example.explanation: Coherence measures how well wave parts keep the relation needed to interfere. Losing excited states already weakens it. Random timing changes weaken it more. In this constant-rate model, coherence cannot last longer than twice the characteristic time for the excited population to fall.

example.title: Two decay times
steps: The population-decay rate is 0.4 per nanosecond and the extra phase-noise rate is 0.1 per nanosecond.
Population lifetime is 2.5 ns; coherence lifetime is 1/(0.2 + 0.1), about 3.33 ns, below 5 ns.

terms.definition: Population-decay lifetime.
Coherence-decay lifetime.
Extra phase-noise rate.
The model’s present change depends on its present state, not its detailed past.
Nanosecond, one billionth of a second.
A definite relation between quantum wave parts that lets the parts interfere in suitable measurements.

incident-flux-counts.idea: To estimate how many particles scatter each second, count the incoming particles and the targets they can hit.
incident-flux-counts.explanation: Flux is the number of particles arriving each second on each square metre. Cross section acts like an effective area for one target. Multiply the flux by that area and the number of targets. This simple count works for a thin sample in which very few particles scatter twice or get removed from the beam.

example.title: A dilute target sample
steps: Use 2 × 10⁸ targets, flux 5 × 10¹⁴ per square metre per second and cross section 3 × 10⁻²⁴ square metres.
The rate is 0.30 per second, giving an expected count of 3 in ten seconds. The actual count can differ.

incident-flux-counts.equation: expected rate = target count × incident flux × cross section

terms.definition: An effective scattering area, not necessarily a target’s geometric size.

outgoing-scattering-amplitude.idea: A scattering amplitude tells how strongly a particle wave spreads in one chosen direction.
outgoing-scattering-amplitude.explanation: Picture a small detector facing the source. Twice as far away, the same patch of directions covers four times as much area. The scattered wave’s probability density falls to one quarter. These changes balance. Squaring the amplitude’s size gives the effective scattering area per unit of solid angle, a measure of the patch of directions.

example.title: One isotropic amplitude
steps: At the stated wave number, the amplitude is (0.5 + 0.5i) nm in every direction.
Its squared size is 0.5² + 0.5² = 0.50 nm², giving differential cross section 0.50 nm² per steradian.

terms.definition: Complex scattering amplitude, measured in length.
Scattering cross section per small patch of directions.
The unit of solid angle.
The imaginary unit.
A change in motion, direction or wave pattern after an interaction. A detector can record how much goes in each direction.
A number for the wave scattered in a chosen direction. In this convention, squaring its size gives the cross section per unit solid angle, an effective area per patch of direction.
An effective area that measures how likely a particular interaction is under the stated conditions.

solid-angle-cross-section.idea: Some patches on a sphere cover more directions than others.
solid-angle-cross-section.explanation: Draw latitude bands of the same width on a globe. A band near a pole covers less area than one at the equator. Count that area difference when adding scattered particles over directions. A solid angle measures the size of such a patch as seen from the centre.

example.title: Integrating one angular distribution
steps: The fit is A(1 + 2cos²θ), with A = 0.30 nm² per steradian.
The full-sphere integral is 4π × 0.30 × (1 + 2/3), or 2π nm², about 6.283 nm².

solid-angle-cross-section.equation: small solid angle = sin θ × dθ × dφ

terms.definition: Polar angle from the beam direction.
Angle around the beam axis.
Very small steps in those angles.
The fitted cross-section scale.
A patch of directions measured by its area on a unit sphere.
A way of adding many small pieces to find a total. Adding small pieces of distance can give the length of a whole trip.

outgoing-green-response.idea: Knowing the wave sent out by one tiny source helps us predict the wave from a whole region.
outgoing-green-response.explanation: The rule for one ideal point source is called a Green function. Use that rule at many source locations and add their contributions. At the source point the ideal expression becomes unbounded, so use it within the sum over space rather than as an ordinary measured number.

example.title: One point away from the source
steps: Take distance 2 nm and wave number π/(2 nm), so the phase angle is π.
The outgoing response is −1/(8π nm), about −0.03979 per nanometre.

terms.definition: The chosen outgoing response kernel.
Distance from the source.
Wave number.
The imaginary unit.
A complex phase factor with angle kr.

scattering-integral-equation.idea: To find a scattered wave, we need to know what the wave does inside the region where it feels a force.
scattering-integral-equation.explanation: Each part of that region contributes an outward-going wave. Their total depends on the wave inside, which is itself affected by scattering. A first guess can make the calculation easier. Its accuracy depends on how much that guess misses.

example.title: One sampled source cell
steps: After all unit factors, one cell contributes 0.001 + 0.0005i to the response integral.
With the chosen outgoing-kernel convention, its correction is −0.001 − 0.0005i. One sampled cell is not a converged scattering solution.

scattering-integral-equation.equation: total wave = incident wave − summed potential response

terms.definition: The imaginary unit.
The response rule linking a source point to an observation point.
A change in motion, direction or wave pattern after an interaction. A detector can record how much goes in each direction.
A way of adding many small pieces to find a total. Adding small pieces of distance can give the length of a whole trip.

packets-and-elastic-regime.idea: A localized incoming packet contains a range of energies.
packets-and-elastic-regime.explanation: A single-energy scattering result is useful only if the scattering amplitude changes little across that range. A narrow wave-number spread helps, but a nearby resonance or threshold can still make the energy dependence important.

example.title: A narrow momentum packet
steps: The mean wave number is 2 per nanometre and its standard deviation is 0.050 per nanometre.
The relative energy spread is about 2 × 0.050/2 = 0.05, or 5%. Check the scattering response over that band.

packets-and-elastic-regime.equation: relative energy spread ≈ 2 × relative wave-number spread

terms.definition: A measure of how widely values spread around their average.
Momentum divided by ℏ.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
A change in motion, direction or wave pattern after an interaction. A detector can record how much goes in each direction.
A number for the wave scattered in a chosen direction. In this convention, squaring its size gives the cross section per unit solid angle, an effective area per patch of direction.

legendre-radial-bridge.idea: Two different wave patterns can overlap in one direction yet cancel in a sum over all directions.
legendre-radial-bridge.explanation: Imagine combining a pattern that stays the same with one that changes from negative to positive. In the overlap sum, equal positive and negative contributions cancel. This is called orthogonality. The angular patterns used here are called Legendre polynomials. The cancellation applies when the calculation includes all directions.

example.title: The first two angular patterns
steps: The first patterns are 1 and u, where u = cos θ.
Their overlap from u = −1 to 1 is zero: the negative half cancels the positive half. This is an amplitude overlap, not a negative probability.

terms.definition: Angle from the beam direction.
Zero integrated overlap between different patterns.
Add the contributions continuously across the stated interval.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

elastic-phase-shifts.idea: A collision can keep the wave’s energy the same but change where its cycle starts.
elastic-phase-shifts.explanation: This kind of collision is called elastic. Compare a wave that felt the force with one that traveled freely. Their peaks can end up shifted even though the incoming and outgoing flows balance. Each angular wave pattern can have its own shift.

example.title: A phase shift of 30°
steps: The phase shift is δ = π/6, so the scattering factor is exp(iπ/3) = ½ + i√3/2.
Its squared size is ¼ + ¾ = 1, consistent with equal incoming and outgoing flow.

terms.definition: Outgoing-to-incoming factor relative to the free-wave reference.
The radial phase shift.
The imaginary unit.
A unit-size complex number with phase angle α.
A change in motion, direction or wave pattern after an interaction. A detector can record how much goes in each direction.

partial-wave-amplitude.idea: Different wave patterns can arrive together at one detector and strengthen or cancel each other.
partial-wave-amplitude.explanation: A partial wave is one part of the full wave with a particular pattern across directions. Each contributes a number with both size and timing. For one detector direction, add those numbers before squaring. Leaving out a large part changes the answer.

example.title: Adding s and p waves forward
steps: In the stated two-channel sample, the forward amplitude is (0.75 + 1.25i) nm.
Squaring its size gives 0.75² + 1.25² = 2.125 nm² per steradian. This uses the combined amplitude.

partial-wave-amplitude.equation: directional cross section = |sum of angular-channel amplitudes|²

terms.definition: Orbital angular channels with labels 0 and 1.
The imaginary unit.
The unit for a patch of directions.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

partial-total-cross-section.idea: To find the total scattering, count outgoing particles in every direction.
partial-total-cross-section.explanation: Different angular wave patterns can interfere in one direction. But when all directions are included, the positive and negative overlap between distinct patterns cancels. Their separate scattering areas then add. A limit on one pattern’s contribution does not limit how many patterns there may be.

example.title: Adding two integrated channels
steps: At the chosen wave number and phase shifts, the s contribution is π nm² and the p contribution is 12π nm².
The total is 13π nm², about 40.84 nm². The addition is justified after integrating all directions.

partial-total-cross-section.equation: total cross section = sum of integrated angular-channel cross sections

terms.definition: Orbital angular channels with labels 0 and 1.
An effective area that measures how likely a particular interaction is under the stated conditions.

optical-theorem.idea: The wave scattered straight ahead gives a clue to how much of the incoming beam scatters in all directions.
optical-theorem.explanation: In the forward direction, the incoming and scattered waves overlap. Their interference accounts for the change in the forward beam. Here particles keep their energy and none are absorbed. The optical theorem connects the total scattering to the imaginary part of the forward amplitude, the number multiplying i.

example.title: Checking an isotropic s wave
steps: At wave number 0.50 per nanometre, the forward amplitude has imaginary part 1.5 nm.
The forward rule gives 4π × 1.5/0.50 = 12π nm². Integrating the uniform angular value 3 nm² per steradian gives the same total.

optical-theorem.equation: total elastic cross section = (4π/k) × Im f(0)

terms.definition: Incident wave number.
Imaginary part of the forward scattering amplitude in the stated outgoing-wave convention.
The orbital angular channel with label zero.
Wave contributions can strengthen or cancel when they meet. Quantum amplitudes can do this, too.
A change in motion, direction or wave pattern after an interaction. A detector can record how much goes in each direction.
A number for the wave scattered in a chosen direction. In this convention, squaring its size gives the cross section per unit solid angle, an effective area per patch of direction.

s-wave-scattering-length.idea: A slow particle’s scattered wave can be summarized by a distance called the scattering length.
s-wave-scattering-length.explanation: Beyond the short reach of the force, extend the nearly zero-energy radial wave’s straight-line form backward. The point where that line would meet zero gives the scattering length. This constructed distance can be negative even though a measured area is always zero or positive.

example.title: An attractive spherical well
steps: The well radius is 2 nm and the dimensionless depth parameter is q = π/4.
The scattering length is 2(1 − 4/π) nm, about −0.5465 nm. Its negative sign belongs to the wave’s extrapolated zero.

terms.definition: Scattering length.
Well radius.
The interior zero-energy wave number multiplied by the radius.
A change in motion, direction or wave pattern after an interaction. A detector can record how much goes in each direction.

partial-wave-resonance.idea: A small change in incoming energy can make one wave pattern scatter much more strongly.
partial-wave-resonance.explanation: A narrow peak in the response is called a resonance. Its width tells us the energy range over which the effect is strong. Here one isolated peak dominates and particles keep their energy. To use the same peak shape for scattering area, the incoming wave spacing must also barely change across it.

example.title: A narrow s-wave resonance
steps: The resonance energy is 100 meV, its full width is 2 meV and the central wave number is 1 per nanometre.
The peak area is about 4π nm². At 101 meV, one half-width away, it is about 2π nm² in the constant-wave-number approximation.

terms.definition: Full energy width at half the phase-factor peak height.
One thousandth of an electronvolt.
The orbital angular channel with label zero.
A result close enough to use when the stated conditions hold. For example, treating a nearly flat road as level can simplify a short-trip calculation.

identical-particle-scattering.idea: When two outgoing particles are identical, counting their two hits as separate collisions doubles the answer.
identical-particle-scattering.explanation: Swapping which particle went to which detector does not label a new event. Combine the two wave alternatives with the sign required for the prepared state. Then count each opposite pair of directions once, for example by summing over one half of the sphere.

example.title: Identical spinless bosons in an s wave
steps: The direct amplitude is (0.5 + 0.5i) nm, and exchange gives the same amplitude.
Their sum has squared size 2 nm². Integrating over one hemisphere gives pair-event cross section 4π nm².

identical-particle-scattering.equation: pair-event area = hemisphere integral of |direct + exchanged amplitude|²

terms.definition: Particles whose full quantum state is symmetric under exchange.
The orbital angular channel with label zero.

first-born-fourier.idea: A first estimate of scattering uses the undisturbed incoming wave inside the region where the force acts.
first-born-fourier.explanation: This is the first Born approximation. Add the small contributions from different parts of that region, including how their wave cycles line up. If the interaction strongly changes the wave there, the original wave is a poor starting guess.

example.title: A weak spherical barrier forward
steps: The barrier has radius 2 nm and the stated strength ratio 0.060.
The first Born forward amplitude is −0.040 nm. Squaring gives 0.0016 nm² per steradian, a forward value rather than the full total.

first-born-fourier.equation: forward differential cross section ≈ |Born forward amplitude|²

terms.definition: The first estimate obtained by using the incoming wave inside the scattering integral.
