central-born-integral.idea: A beam that turns through a larger angle changes its momentum more, even if its speed stays the same.
central-born-integral.explanation: Momentum includes direction. Imagine two arrows of equal length, one for the incoming motion and one for the outgoing motion. With their tails together, the distance between their tips gives the size of the momentum change. Straight ahead gives zero change.

example.title: A 60° scattering angle
steps: The incident wave number is 2 per nanometre and the scattering angle is π/3.
The transfer wave number is 2 × 2 × sin(π/6) = 2 per nanometre. Physical momentum transfer is ℏ times this value.

terms.definition: Transfer wave number.
Incident and outgoing wave-number size.
Angle between incoming and outgoing directions.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
A change in motion, direction or wave pattern after an interaction. A detector can record how much goes in each direction.

gaussian-born-example.idea: A smooth force pattern can make a beam scatter most strongly near its original direction.
gaussian-born-example.explanation: The potential in this example is shaped like a bell. The first Born estimate uses the incoming wave to add the effect of each part of the bell. At larger angles the wave contributions cancel more. Their combined size falls, and the area for scattering falls with its square.

example.title: At transfer qa = 2
steps: The model’s forward angular cross section is about 0.00502655 nm² per steradian.
At qa = 2, multiply it by e^(−2), giving about 0.000680269 nm² per steradian. This still assumes the Born approximation is valid.

terms.definition: Transfer wave number.
The Gaussian potential’s length scale.
e raised to x, with e about 2.718.
A change in motion, direction or wave pattern after an interaction. A detector can record how much goes in each direction.
An effective area that measures how likely a particular interaction is under the stated conditions.

screened-potential-example.idea: If the force has a shorter reach, a beam scatters differently, even straight ahead.
screened-potential-example.explanation: In this model the interaction fades rapidly beyond a distance called the screening length. That fade keeps the predicted wave scattered straight ahead finite. Extending the interaction farther and farther can make this prediction grow without a limit. A long-range interaction needs a different treatment.

example.title: One finite screening scale
steps: For the stated model with length scale 2 nm, the forward amplitude is −0.080 nm.
At qa = 1 it is −0.040 nm, half the amplitude and one quarter of the forward angular cross section.

terms.definition: Transfer wave number.
The finite screening length in this example.
Reduction of an interaction’s effect over long distances.
A number for the wave scattered in a chosen direction. In this convention, squaring its size gives the cross section per unit solid angle, an effective area per patch of direction.
An effective area that measures how likely a particular interaction is under the stated conditions.

born-error-and-unitarity.idea: We can test a scattering shortcut by comparing its prediction with an exact answer for the same beam and target.
born-error-and-unitarity.explanation: The Born shortcut starts with the wave the beam would have if the target did not disturb it. Try it on a weak interaction whose full solution is known. Subtract the two predictions and compare that difference with the size of the exact answer. A wave effect left out by the shortcut can matter when checking that all particles are accounted for.

example.title: A weak attractive well
steps: For depth parameter 0.30, exact matching gives scattering length divided by radius about −0.0311208.
The Born estimate is −0.0300000. The absolute error is about 0.0011208 times the radius, roughly 3.60% of the exact length’s size.

born-error-and-unitarity.equation: absolute error = |approximate scattering length − exact scattering length|

terms.definition: The result from replacing the interior wave by the incoming wave.
A change in motion, direction or wave pattern after an interaction. A detector can record how much goes in each direction.

static-approximation-capstone.idea: A shortcut needs a small comparison number. Find that number before trusting the answer.
static-approximation-capstone.explanation: For two separated energy levels, divide the strength of their link by the gap between their energies. A small result supports estimating the shift from the original levels. Compare that estimate with the exact two-level answer to see how well it worked here.

example.title: Checking one weak coupling
steps: The gap is 5 eV and the coupling 0.20 eV, giving ratio 0.04.
The second-order lower shift is −0.20²/5 = −0.008 eV. Exact diagonalization gives about −0.00798724 eV, a difference about 0.00001276 eV.

terms.definition: Finding the states on which the energy matrix acts by simple multiplication.
One amount divided by another. Three red counters for every two blue gives a red-to-blue ratio of 3/2.

driven-open-capstone.idea: A system that can switch back and forth needs a different rule from one that can only lose energy to its surroundings.
driven-open-capstone.explanation: In the first case, the drive can move probability into one state and back out again. A shortcut that only counts the first small transfer works briefly. In the second case a constant loss rate can describe decay. First identify which experiment the numbers describe.

example.title: Testing a short closed-system drive
steps: The drive rate is 2 radians per second and it acts for 0.20 seconds. The formula uses half of rate × time, so the angle inside the sine is 2 × 0.20 ÷ 2 = 0.20 radians.
The exact transfer is sin²(0.20), about 0.03947. Its weak estimate, 0.04000, is close for this duration.

terms.definition: The specified two-state rotation rate.
Duration.
Evolution retaining the relative phases needed for interference.

quantum3-assessment.idea: To check whether every scattered particle was counted, find the total scattering in two ways.
quantum3-assessment.explanation: First add what goes out in all directions. Then use the change in the wave moving straight ahead, where the incoming and scattered waves meet. For this model no particle disappears or changes its internal energy. The two totals should agree if every contribution was counted correctly.

example.title: One s-plus-p conservation check
steps: With wave number 1.5 per nanometre and the given phases, the angular-channel sum is 40π/9 nm².
The forward imaginary amplitude is 5/3 nm, so 4π × (5/3)/1.5 gives the same 40π/9, about 13.96 nm².

quantum3-assessment.equation: integrated elastic area = (4π/k) × imaginary forward amplitude
